about: The content address — RFC-002 §5's `Proposal.id`, the name a proposal has
that nothing else can give it.
sha256:<64 lower-case hex>  over  canonicalJson({ author, ops, parent })
THREE FIELDS. `surface` and `intent` are deliberately NOT in the pre-image,
and that exclusion is the whole content of the fixture. RFC-002 §4.1: the
door takes `{parents, ops}` and not provenance, 'so a chat-authored change
and a click-authored change are indistinguishable downstream — enforced by
the signature, not by review discipline'. §9.1 makes that mechanical: a
scripted click and a scripted chat that author the same change must produce
the same id. `same_address` below is that gate, as data.
⚠ The address is NOT a hash of the stored `canonical` bytes. Those carry
`surface` and `intent` on purpose — provenance is KEPT, it just does not get
a vote. Hashing the stored line would give the two surfaces different ids and
quietly invert §9.1.
⛔ `author` IS in the pre-image, and that is not a contradiction. It is
invariant ⑤ (nothing is attributed to nobody): two people proposing the same
words are making two proposals, each of which one of them is answerable for.
What §9.1 collapses is the surface, never the person.
`pre_image` is pinned as well as `address` because a digest that disagrees
tells you only THAT two implementations differ; the bytes tell you WHERE.
Three implementations execute these cases, each canonicalizing independently:
console/lib/address.ts (vitest), services/spec/src/proposal.rs (cargo test),
and conformance/check_conformance.py, which canonicalizes in stdlib Python
and hashes with hashlib rather than trusting either.

cases.name: a_different_read_point_is_a_different_proposal
cases.why: The parent is what the author was looking at. The same words against a corpus that has moved are a different judgement, and RFC-002 §5 makes the read point part of the id for exactly that reason.

cases.name: the_same_two_ops_in_the_other_order
cases.why: ⛔ Ops are ORDERED (§5) — they are applied in sequence and reviewed in sequence. Swapping them is a different proposal, so it must be a different address. A set-hash here would silently merge two reviews.

cases.name: a_kernel_op_is_addressed_like_any_other
cases.why: declarePrecedence needs kernel capability, so this proposal is QUEUED rather than admitted. A queued proposal is still a proposal and still has a name — the verdict is recorded beside the address, never instead of it.

cases.name: text_outside_ascii_and_the_two_escapes
cases.why: The pre-image is UTF-8 with JSON's own escaping and nothing else: a non-ASCII character stays raw, a quote and a backslash are escaped. Both implementations must agree byte for byte or the same proposal gets two names.

same_address.name: click_and_chat_and_an_mcp_client_are_one_proposal
same_address.why: §9.1's equal-citizen gate. Three surfaces, three intents, one change — one address. If these ever differ the surfaces are composing different ops and the claim that they are one system is false.

different_address.name: the_read_point_the_author_saw
different_address.why: A proposal made against a corpus that has moved is a different proposal.

different_address.name: who_is_answerable_for_it
different_address.why: ⑤ — the person does not collapse.

different_address.name: ops_are_ordered_not_a_set
different_address.why: ⛔ Ops are applied in sequence and reviewed in sequence. A set-hash would silently merge two different reviews into one name.
